# No clutch fluid flows out through the slave cylinder bleed valve and no resistance in clutch

When a hydraulic clutch pedal drops to the floor instantly, offering zero resistance, you are facing a catastrophic loss of pressure. In the context of your 1986 Toyota Corona sedan (L-KT147V-TXKDS), this specific behaviorâcombined with the observation that no fluid exits the slave cylinder bleed valve despite a full master reservoirâpoints directly to an internal failure within the hydraulic circuit rather than a simple external leak.

The mechanics of your system rely on the master cylinder pushing hydraulic fluid through the line to the slave cylinder. The slave cylinder then converts this fluid pressure into linear motion via its piston, which pushes the clutch fork to disengage the release bearing from the pressure plate springs. If there is no resistance felt at the pedal, the hydraulic column has collapsed. This usually happens because the system cannot build or maintain the necessary pressure to move the slave piston against the friction of the return spring and the mechanical load of the clutch assembly.

Your first observation rules out external gasket failures. If the seal on the master cylinder was blown, fluid would likely be visible on the transmission bell housing or dripping from the master cylinder body itself. Similarly, a failed slave cylinder seal typically results in puddles around the engine bay near the firewall. Since you see no external oil leaks, the fluid is being trapped inside the system, but not moving.

The second observationâthe absence of fluid at the bleed valve when the reservoir is fullâis the critical diagnostic clue. When you loosen the bleed nut on a functional slave cylinder while the master reservoir is topped off, gravity and residual pressure should force fluid out immediately. The fact that nothing comes out indicates one of two scenarios: either the master cylinder piston has failed internally, or the slave cylinder piston has seized in a way that prevents fluid displacement entirely.

Consider the internal structure of the master cylinder. These units often use a rubber cup seal that can degrade over time. If this seal tears, hydraulic fluid bypasses the piston and enters the return chamber. When you press the pedal, the fluid simply moves from the reservoir side to the return side without building pressure at the outlet port. Consequently, the slave cylinder never actuates. This explains why the clutch fork remains engaged; the hydraulic push is missing entirely. The lack of fluid exiting the slave bleed nut confirms that the source of pressure (the master) is compromised or the line is blocked, rather than the slave leaking internally.

Alternatively, the slave cylinder piston could be seized. If the internal bore of the slave cylinder is corroded or if the piston has welded to the bore due to heat and age (common in 1986 models), the piston cannot move regardless of how much pressure you apply. In this specific case, fluid *would* still flow out of the master cylinder side if you were to remove the bleeder screw on the master cylinder itself, but the slave cylinder would remain dead weight. However, given that no fluid comes out of the slave bleed nut, it is highly probable that the fluid never reached the slave or was bypassed by a blown master cup.

The third observation regarding the clutch fork provides further context. The fork not returning suggests that the hydraulic pressure isn't just insufficient to engage the clutch; it might be that the mechanical linkage is binding or that the slave cylinder's internal return spring has collapsed along with the piston seal. If the master cylinder is bypassing internally, the fluid volume simply doesn't shift enough to overcome the friction of the fork mechanism, leaving it stuck in a partially engaged position until the pedal is fully depressed and the system depressurizes completely.

To resolve this on your Corona, you must replace the component that failed to build pressure. Since external leaks are absent and no fluid exits the slave bleed nut, the master cylinder is the prime suspect for internal bypassing. Replacing the master cylinder will restore the hydraulic column's integrity, allowing fluid to pressurize the line and move the slave piston correctly. If the master cylinder replacement does not resolve the issue, then the slave cylinder is likely seized internally and requires replacement as well. Always bleed the system thoroughly after replacing any component to ensure no air pockets mimic a pressure loss, though in this case, the mechanical failure of a seal is the root cause.
